title: Here’s the latest on the 2026 DealBook Summit.
text:
DealBook Summit Live Updates: OpenAI Executives Speaking at Gathering of Business and Political Leaders
Sam Altman and Greg Brockman of OpenAI are onstage now with Andrew Ross Sorkin. Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, Elon Musk and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York are expected later.
Latest
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said it was “hard to imagine the A.I. industry” without Jensen Huang, the former Nvidia chief executive who stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a tech executive who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset. Mr. Altman said at the DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday that Mr. Huang, whose company has been a driving force of investment in the sector, “took one of the earliest big bets on us.”
Mr. Altman spoke alongside Greg Brockman, the chief executive and president of OpenAI, during an interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin, as part of a day of interviews with worldwide newsmakers. The discussions with Mr. Sorkin, a New York Times columnist and the founder of the DealBook newsletter, are expected to touch on many other pressing issues, including an election that swung the balance of power in Congress and a global economy roiled by President Trump’s trade war and high energy prices.
The day’s lineup includes Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX; Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York. Vice President JD Vance will not appear as scheduled.
The first interview of the day was with Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, who said running the World Economic Forum “is one of the options” for what she will do after she steps down in February. She also discussed frustrations with capitalism around the world, even as companies attain sky-high valuations. “I think it raises the question of who is benefiting, how that creation of value will be shared and distributed,” she said.
Here’s the rest of this year’s lineup (conversations that will be carried here live are noted in parentheses):
Morning session:
- Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada (livestream)
- David Ellison, chief executive of Skydance (livestream)
- Hailey Bieber, founder of Rhode
Afternoon session, beginning at 1:50 p.m.:
- Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries
- Adena Friedman, chief executive of Nasdaq; Vlad Tenev, chief executive of Robinhood; Shayne Coplan, chief executive of Polymarket
- Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York (livestream)
- Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft
- Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla (livestream)
“We plan to be a public company at some point,” Altman said. While Anthropic is expected to go public in a blockbuster I.P.O. tomorrow, OpenAI executives have said the company will delay its public offering until next year to focus on safety issues.
“The models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment— that’s new,” Brockman said. “That’s actually been a huge cultural shift.”
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, and Greg Brockman, the company’s president, have joined Andrew on stage. Andrew asked what they thought about the ouster of Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia. “Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us,” Altman said. “We took a big bet on Nvidia. It’s hard to imagine the A.I. industry without Jensen.” He added, “I have a little more empathy towards the situation than the average person.” Altman was briefly pushed out of OpenAI in 2023 in what has become known as the “the blip.”
Lagarde said running the World Economic Forum, which hosts the influential annual gathering in Davos, Switzerland, “is one of the options” for what she will do next. But she didn’t hint at other options, saying she wasn’t going to entertain more speculation while she is still E.C.B. president. She holds that position until Feb. 7.
Lagarde talked about the resilience of the European economy and said A.I. investment and government spending has supported it. She added that reforms are still necessary, including making it easier to get capital to European entrepreneurs and move toward a fiscal union. Europe has to “beef up its game and fast,” she said.
Lagarde answered a question about frustrations with capitalism. She alluded to the Anthropic I.P.O. taking place tomorrow, which is set to value the company at more than $1 trillion, making it one of the largest public listings ever. “There are significant valuations being determined, significant I.P.O.s being declared,” she said. “And I think it raises the question of who is benefiting, how that creation of value will be shared and distributed.”
Christine Lagarde spoke about her decision to step down from the E.C.B. in February. She said trust was in “short supply” at the moment, and she felt it was her duty to speak up against fake news and misrepresentations in political campaigns. She didn’t clarify where she will direct her attention, but there is an important presidential election taking place in her home country of France next spring.
As president of the European Central Bank, Christine Lagarde has also been managing the fallout of the war in Iran. Europe is a big energy importer and experienced a sharp increase in inflation because of the conflict. In the summer, the E.C.B. was the first major central bank to raise interest rates in response to the war and might do a third increase next month. It really shows how widespread the implications of this conflict have been and I’m sure she’ll talk about it because ending the war is also essential for Europe’s economic outlook. So I’m interested in her assessment of the risk that inflation continues to worsen in Europe and how much more the central bank might need to do. At the same time, higher interest rates will need to be balanced against concerns that Europe’s economic resilience could be tested.
Meredith Kopit Levien, the chief executive of The New York Times, just kicked off the event. The audience — including big names in business, media and technology — has filed into the packed auditorium. Levien noted that it’s the 25th anniversary of DealBook and the 175th anniversary of The Times.
I’m looking forward to hearing David Ellison talk, a little over a month after his company Skydance finally closed its deal with Warner Bros. Discovery. One of Ellison’s biggest challenges will be navigating the company’s roughly $80 billion debt load. I want to hear how he will handle servicing that debt, cutting costs, and still investing in the company.
I also want to hear Ellison reflect a bit about his efforts to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, which at times put the company in political crosshairs, and how he is thinking about the company’s relationship with the government. Just this week, President Trump took aim at the management at CBS News.
This year’s DealBook Summit comes amid heightened uncertainty in corporate America and in Washington, where voter anxiety over economic pressures helped drive a resetting of the political balance of power two weeks ago.
Will the Democrats’ resounding midterm elections victory lead to tougher oversight of businesses, especially Big Tech? Can either party muster the political will to tackle voters’ biggest grievances — namely, the rising cost of living and the rapid spread of data centers in communities across the nation?
Wall Street and Silicon Valley have big concerns, too. Is the latest market sell-off a blip, or a sign that the artificial intelligence rally has run out of steam? Speaking of A.I., will the resignation of Jensen Huang, a founder at Nvidia and the face of the high-flying sector, trigger a drought in deals and investment?
These questions and more will dominate the discussion on Wednesday as Andrew Ross Sorkin, DealBook’s founder, interviews leaders in business, policy and culture.
The morning sessions will feature separate interviews with Christine Lagarde, the European Central Bank’s president, and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada. Global trade and President Trump’s tariffs will be on the agenda.
U.S. politics will be in focus during interviews with Vice President JD Vance and New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani.
A.I. will be a big theme throughout the day, especially during Mr. Sorkin’s discussion with Sam Altman and Greg Brockman of OpenAI, which is expected to go public some time next year.
Later in the day, Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, a major investor in OpenAI, will speak on the topic, too.
And Elon Musk, whose business empire and personal fortune hinges on the technology, will be the final interview of the day.
Hailey Bieber, the model and entrepreneur who sold her Rhode beauty brand in a deal worth at least $800 million last year, will offer a view into her real-world business — built on products that can be felt and applied to a person’s face — during a day that will spend lots of time focused on A.I. and technology.
Bieber is a master of social media and she has used platforms like Instagram, where she has nearly 60 million followers, to successfully promote peptide lip tints and liquids that promise a trendy “glazed donut” look to young women. Rhode, which she co-founded with Lauren and Michael D. Ratner in 2022, has become a bigger sensation since its sale to E.L.F. Beauty, which helped it expand to Sephora stores. Bieber, who is married to the pop star Justin Bieber and is a daughter of the actor Stephen Baldwin, remains Rhode’s chief creative officer and head of innovation.
While OpenAI has delayed its initial public offering plans till next year, the conversation with its two most visible faces — chief executive Sam Altman and Greg Brockman, the company president who has taken a more active role in its day-to-day operations — comes as its rival Anthropic is slated for a blockbuster I.P.O. tomorrow. It’ll be interesting to hear from the pair on how OpenAI is seeking to catch up to Anthropic’s lead while it deals with rogue A.I. hacks, high-profile executive departures and public backlash against data centers, which provide the much-needed computing power to build and run its product.
Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, is one of the few non-Americans in the lineup today. Though she’s a central banker and her primary job is managing inflation in the eurozone, Lagarde is outspoken on Europe’s role in the world and how the continent can strengthen its autonomy and competitiveness. Some reforms could lessen Europe’s ties with and dependency on the United States, so I’m really interested to hear what message she will have for a more American audience.
Lagarde is also in her last few months as president of the E.C.B. because she has chosen to step down early. I wonder if we’ll get any hints about what she will do next. She’s previously said she wanted to be able to shed the political neutrality that comes with the E.C.B role.
DealBook, founded 25 years ago by The New York Times columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin, breaks down the most important business news of the day for leaders on Wall Street, in Washington, and beyond.
DealBook has been a key part of The Times’s daily news report with scoops and in-depth features for a quarter century. And since 2012, the DealBook team has organized the DealBook Summit, a major annual news event where Mr. Sorkin has interviewed scores of newsmakers.
Summit newsmakers over the years have included Elon Musk; Jensen Huang, the former C.E.O. of Nvidia; JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon; the former vice president, Kamala Harris; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and Volodymyr Zelensky, the president of Ukraine.
Mr. Sorkin, who began writing for The Times when he was still in high school, has broken major stories including Chase’s acquisition of J.P. Morgan and Hewlett-Packard’s takeover of Compaq. In May, he broke the news that the Treasury Department was making a complicated addition to so-called Trump accounts: allowing wealthy individuals to donate shares of their companies.
As a columnist for The Times, Mr. Sorkin has frequently examined how corporate America and financial firms can leverage their market heft to address gun violence. His reporting has focused particular attention on proposals for credit card transaction tracking, and merchant category codes to better monitor gun sales.
Mr. Sorkin is the author of two books: “1929: Inside the Greatest Crash in Wall Street History — and How It Shattered a Nation” and “Too Big to Fail,” a chronicle of the 2008 global financial crisis. He has won two Gerald Loeb Awards, a marquee prize in business journalism, and helped create the Showtime television series “Billions.” He is also an anchor on the CNBC financial news program “Squawk Box.”
Artificial intelligence. Wars and tariffs. Crypto and digital finance. The new generation of influencers transforming the media landscape. Corporate leadership in an age of political and economic uncertainty.
In interview after interview, I’ve tackled all that and more over the years at the DealBook Summit.
As we celebrate the 25th anniversary of DealBook, I’m excited about what we have planned for you today: unfiltered conversations with Vice President JD Vance, Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Zohran Mamdani and many more.
Over the years, I have brought together scores of leaders from the world of business, politics and culture for candid — sometimes blunt — discussions of the top issues of the day. We’ve made plenty of news.
Take last year. We again gathered prominent figures from Washington, corporate America and more. They included Anthropic’s Dario Amodei; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; Mr. Beast, Mary Barra, General Motors’ chief executive; and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California to discuss the issues moving markets, rewriting the rules of global trade and shaking up the media world.
It’s a setting where even diverse viewpoints can illuminate where the big stories will take us next. It also signals the power players to watch, and the changes they are looking to bring to business and society.
People still stop me to ask about my 2023 interview with Mr. Musk, which was punctuated with an expletive aimed at advertisers pulling back from his social media platform, but also covered a frank discussion on his views about everything from antisemitism to power and what drives him.
In 2024, Jeff Bezos told me of his hopeful view for President Trump’s second term. That comment may have surprised the public. But Mr. Bezos signaled on the stage what would become a defining aspect of the Trump administration: Big Tech’s embrace of him and his embrace of Big Tech.
In 2022, Sam Bankman-Fried offered up a mea culpa just days before his arrest for the collapse of his crypto exchange.
Two world leaders — Volodymyr Zelensky, the president of Ukraine, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel — spoke to us in the middle of wars.
I’ve got plenty more questions to ask. Stay tuned.
This year’s DealBook Summit will include interviews with some of the most powerful people from politics Silicon Valley and Washington.
Here are the guests speaking with DealBook’s founder, Andrew Ross Sorkin:
Elon Musk is the founder, chief executive and chief engineer of SpaceX, and the chief executive of Tesla. Mr. Musk also oversaw the Department of Government Efficiency, an aggressive Trump administration effort to slash spending and the federal work force, and donated nearly a half-billon dollars to Republicans during the midterm election cycle.
Mark Carney is the prime minister of Canada. Mr. Carney took office in March 2025 amid a trade fight with the United States that arose from President Trump’s aggressive tariff policies.
Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of New York City. Mr. Mamdani’s progressive agenda — including the imposition of a tax on second homes, a rent-freeze on nearly one million rent-stabilized apartments and the expansion of free child care — has been greeted with both objections from many in the business community, and attempts to reach a kind of détente.
Christine Lagarde is the president of the European Central Bank. Ms. Lagarde, who will leave her post in February, has overseen fiscal policy at the central bank through economic crises including the Covid-19 pandemic and two energy shocks.
Sam Altman is a founder and the chief executive of OpenAI, the A.I. research company behind ChatGPT. Mr. Altman’s company has drawn scrutiny for rogue actions by its artificial intelligence agents, which has fueled a contentious debate over A.I. safety.
Greg Brockman is a founder and the president of OpenAI. He and Mr. Altman testified earlier this year in a trial that pitted Mr. Musk against OpenAI, which Mr. Musk helped found in 2015 but left in early 2018 after a power struggle.
Satya Nadella is the chairman and chief executive of Microsoft. Mr. Nadella took over as chief of Microsoft in 2014 and oversaw its early investment in OpenAI, but recently renegotiated the partnership to reduce their dependence on each other. Wall Street is keenly watching Microsoft’s artificial intelligence strategy, which has helped propel it to one of the world’s most valuable companies.
Shayne Coplan is the C.E.O. of Polymarket, the world’s largest prediction market. Mr. Coplan’s company, which is backed by an investment firm partly owned by Donald Trump Jr., has faced regulatory scrutiny amid the sector’s rapid growth.
David Ellison is the chairman and chief executive of Skydance. Mr. Ellison, the son of the Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, oversees a Hollywood behemoth that includes CBS and Paramount following a $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery.
Hailey Bieber is the founder, chief creative officer and head of innovation of Rhode, the No. 1 overall skin care brand in the U.S. by Earned Market Value, and a strategic adviser to e.l.f. Beauty, which acquired Rhode in 2025 for $1 billion.
Adena Friedman is the chair and chief executive of Nasdaq, a leading global exchange and technology company that has become a Wall Street behemoth. Ms. Friedman has led Nasdaq since 2017, and has become a major proponent of tokenized trading of financial assets, including equities.
Palmer Luckey is the founder of the defense technology company Anduril Industries. Mr. Luckey, who founded Anduril after being fired by Facebook in 2017, has won the support of members of the Trump administration with a vision of warfare focused on autonomous weapons.
Vlad Tenev is the chairman and chief executive of Robinhood, the digital brokerage. Mr. Tenev’s company has been at the center of a rapid growth in retail trading, including the frenzy around meme stocks including GameStop, and is among the companies selected to run new Trump accounts for children.
